AgreeLab: AgreeLab help 1/9: Agreement beyond chance
Two raters sort the same N items into k
categories.  Observed agreement po = the
share on the diagonal of the table.
Some agreement happens by chance: if the
raters chose independently at their own
rates, pe = sum of (row share × column share).
Cohen's kappa (1960) = (po - pe)/(1 - pe):
the share of the possible agreement beyond
chance that was reached.  1 = perfect,
0 = chance level, below 0 = worse than chance.
Tiles page: drag a count from an off-diagonal
tile to a diagonal one and watch kappa rise.

AgreeLab help 2/9: SE, CI and the test
Two different SEs (Fleiss, Cohen & Everitt 1969, Psychol Bull
- the large-sample SE gives the 95% CI, kappa ± 1.96 SE (rough
when N is small);
- SE₀, the SE if kappa were 0, gives the test: z = kappa/SE₀,
one-sided p.
p = P(a kappa this big | H₀: kappa = 0).
It is not the chance that H₀ is true, and 'better than chance' is
easy to reach: raters who agree on only 1 item in 3 can reach it.
The CI says how much agreement there is, and how precisely it
is known.
statsmodels' cohens_kappa uses the same SEs.

AgreeLab help 3/9: Kappa max and the paradox
kappa max (Cohen 1960): with these row and
column totals, at most sum of min(row, col)
can agree.  Raters who use the categories at
different rates can never reach kappa = 1.
The paradox (Feinstein & Cicchetti 1990):
high po, low kappa, when one category is
very common: pe is then high too.  Load the
two paradox tables (illustrative numbers):
both have po = 0.85; kappa 0.32 and 0.70.
PABAK = (k po - 1)/(k - 1) (Byrt, Bishop &
Carlin 1993) removes prevalence and bias:
it is po rescaled.  Report po, the margins
and kappa together, not kappa alone.

AgreeLab help 4/9: Weighted kappa
Ordered categories (certain, probable, ...):
a near miss is better than a far one.
Weighted kappa (Cohen 1968) gives tile i, j
the credit w(i, j), 1 on the diagonal:
linear 1 - |i - j|/(k - 1)
(Cicchetti & Allison 1971);
quadratic 1 - (i - j)²/(k - 1)²
(Fleiss & Cohen 1973).
Then po and pe use the weights, and
kappa_w = (po_w - pe_w)/(1 - pe_w); SEs as
for kappa (Fleiss, Cohen & Everitt 1969).
Quadratic weights give the most credit to
near misses.  Choose weights before the data.

AgreeLab help 5/9: Many raters, Fleiss' kappa
Each of N subjects gets m ratings (Fleiss
1971); the raters may differ by subject.
Data: counts n(i, j) = how many put subject i
in category j (each row adds to m).
P_i = share of subject i's m(m-1)/2 rater
pairs that agree; P = their mean.
Pe = sum of p_j², p_j = category j's share.
kappa = (P - Pe)/(1 - Pe); per category too.
SE under H₀ only (Fleiss, Nee & Landis 1979,
Psychol Bull 86:974): a test, but no CI.
Your data: D1-D9 = categories, one row per
subject, every row adding to the same m.

AgreeLab help 6/9: Which ICC?
n targets × k raters, measured values.
ICC = between-target variance / total (Shrout & Fleiss 1979;

scores every target higher lowers it;
(3,1) these raters only: CONSISTENCY.
(1,k), (2,k), (3,k): the reliability of the MEAN of the k raters.
CIs from F (S & F 1979; ICC(2,1) with Satterthwaite's df).

AgreeLab help 7/9: Bland-Altman
Two methods on the same n targets (Bland & Altman 1986,
Lancet i:307): plot d = A - B against the mean (A + B)/2.
bias =
d
, the mean difference; limits of
agreement = bias ± 1.96 s: about 95% of differences fall there.
CI of the bias: bias ± t s/√n.
CI of a limit: ± t s√(1/n + 1.96²/(2(n - 1))), APPROXIMATE
(Bland & Altman 1986 SE). In a review's simulation (40,000 runs)
it covered about 92% at n = 3-5 and 94% at n = 17.
Trend: regress d on the mean; a slope means the two methods
differ more for larger (or smaller) values.
A high r is not agreement: r ignores bias.

AgreeLab help 8/9: Benchmarks are conventions
Landis & Koch (1977, Biometrics 33:159-174)
offered words for ranges of kappa, as
benchmarks:
below 0 poor, 0 - 0.20 slight,
0.61 - 0.80 substantial,
0.81 - 1 almost perfect.
They are a convention, NOT a test: no
p-value or CI stands behind them, and the
same kappa means different things at other
prevalences or numbers of categories.

AgreeLab help 9/9: Agreement and forensic work
Agreement is reliability, not accuracy:
two examiners can agree and both be wrong.
Accuracy needs cases where the truth is
known (ground truth), not a second opinion.
Kappa depends on the mix of cases (the
paradox), so two studies' kappas compare
only if their case mixes are alike.
Kappa assumes independent ratings: a
verifier who knows the first conclusion is
not an independent rater.
A teaching aid only: not validated for
forensic, clinical or legal use.

AnovaLab: AnovaLab help 1/9: What one-way ANOVA asks
H₀: every group has the same population mean μ.
ANOVA splits the total spread (SS) in two:
between: n × (group mean - grand mean)²
within: (value - its own group mean)²
MS = SS / df;  F = MS between / MS within.
If H₀ is true, F is near 1 and follows the
F(k - 1, N - k) curve; p = P(F this big | H₀).
A small p is evidence that SOME mean differs:
not which (Pairs page), not how much (eta²).
eta² = SS between / SS total; omega² (Hays)
subtracts the part chance alone would give.
Every value counts: 0 and negatives are data.

AnovaLab help 2/9: Welch and the checks
The F test assumes equal spreads (and roughly normal groups).
Welch's F (1951) drops equal spreads: each group is weighted
by n / s².
Levene's test (Brown-Forsythe form) runs the one-way F on
|value - group median|; non-normal data affect it little.
Bartlett's χ² compares the s² directly: it is misled by
non-normal data.
In the insect-spray preset, s runs from 1.7 to 6.2 and Levene's
test flags it; compare the ordinary F with Welch's.
A check that is not significant is not proof of equal spreads: with
small groups the checks often miss real differences.

AnovaLab help 6/9: Randomized blocks
Each block (a judge, a person) gets every
treatment once: repeated measures.
Blocks differ a lot, and that spread is taken
OUT of the error: SSE = SST - SSTr - SSBlocks.
F (treatments) = MS treatments / MS error.
partial eta² = SSTr / (SSTr + SSE).
The Table page also shows the one-way F that
ignores the blocks: judges' ratings give
p = 0.048 that way, far smaller with blocks.
Assumes no block × treatment interaction
(and, for repeated measures, sphericity).
Plot: one gray line per block.

AnovaLab help 7/9: One and two variances
One σ: χ² = (n - 1) s² / σ₀², df n - 1.
CI for σ²: ((n-1)s²/χ² upper, (n-1)s²/χ² lower)
Two σ: F = s₁² / s₂², df n₁ - 1 and n₂ - 1.

Two-sided p = 2 × the smaller tail.  The curve
shades that tail and the other tail of EQUAL
area (blue), and both critical regions (red).
These tests trust normal data much more than
tests of means do; skewed data mislead them.

BiNorm3D: BiNorm3D help 1/5: What ρ does
X and Y each follow N(0, 1); ρ is their correlation.  The surface is
their joint density f(x, y): the volume under it is 1.
ρ = 0: a round bell.  Knowing X tells you nothing about Y.
ρ > 0: it stretches along y = x (high x with high y); ρ < 0:
along y = −x.
The volume stays 1, so a narrower bell is a taller one: the peak
Color = height: blue low, then magenta, red at the top.  The
height scale never changes, so the peaks can be
compared across ρ.

BiNorm3D help 2/5: Why the contours tilt
Cont looks straight down.  Each ellipse is a
level of the surface, Q = k², where
Q = (x² − 2ρxy + y²) / (1 − ρ²).
The cross term −2ρxy tilts them: along y = x
the variance is 1 + ρ, across it 1 − ρ.
Q is χ² with 2 df, so the share inside
is 1 − e^(−k²/2): 39 % inside k = 1 and
86 % inside k = 2, whatever ρ is.
The magenta line E[Y | x] = ρx is the
regression line.  It runs through the left
and right ends of every ellipse, not along
the long axis.

BiNorm3D help 3/5: What a slice is
Slice cuts the surface along the line x = x₀.
Scaled to area 1, the cut is the distribution
of Y among the cases that have X = x₀:
Y | X = x₀ is N(ρx₀, √(1 − ρ²)).
Its center ρx₀ lies on the regression line
y = ρx; the SD is the same for every x₀.
The ridge of the bell runs along y = x, but
the slices peak on the flatter magenta line.

BiNorm3D help 4/5: Regression to the mean
Pick the cases with an extreme x₀, say 2 SD
above the mean.  Their average y is ρx₀:
1.2 SD at ρ = 0.6 -- nearer the mean, though
nothing was done to them.  With |ρ| < 1, ρx₀

the stronger the pull.

BurrLab: BurrLab help 1/6: The Burr XII model
The Burr XII is a flexible model for a long
right tail: sentences served, waits to
re-arrest, insurance losses, incomes. Two
shapes C and K and a scale S. Its tail is a
power law: P(X > x) falls like x^(-K C).
The mean exists only if K×C > 1, the variance
only if K×C > 2: with a heavy enough tail the
sample mean never settles down to one value
(menu 4).

CICatcher: CICatcher help 1/6: 95 % of WHAT?
Each line is the interval from ONE sample.
The green line is the truth (μ or p): the method never sees it. A
blue line caught it (the interval contains it); a red line missed it.
The 95 % is the share of intervals the METHOD catches in the
long run, not a property of any one interval. Keep adding
samples: the 'all' rate at the top of the screen settles near the
confidence level.
Any one interval either caught μ or missed it.
So say 'we are 95 % confident' -- meaning the method catches
the truth 95 % of the time -- not 'a 95 % chance μ is in
THIS interval'.

CICatcher help 3/6: Wald and Wilson
Wald:  ± z × √((1 - )/n), the textbook interval. Center and
width both come from , which fails when n × p is small:
at p = 0.10, n = 20 Wald catches only 87.6 % (exact binomial; it
claims 95 %).
12.2 % of those samples have  = 0: the Wald interval has ZERO
width and must miss.
Wilson (score) takes its SE from each possible p, not from ,
and keeps every p within z SEs of : never zero width, center
pulled toward 1/2. Same p and n: 95.7 %.
Wald needs n × p and n × (1 - p) to be 10 or more; at p = 0.10,
n = 100 it reaches 93.2 %.
Gray on the axis: impossible values (below 0, above 1). Only
Wald lines can reach them.

CICatcher help 4/6: Exact intervals
Exact (Clopper-Pearson) uses no normal curve:
it keeps every p for which your count is not in either α/2 tail of
Binomial(n, p).
A count has only n + 1 possible values, so no interval can catch
exactly 95 % at every p.
Exact makes sure it is NEVER LESS: at n = 20 its worst case over
every p is 95.8 %.
At p = 0.10, n = 20 it catches 98.9 % (Wilson 95.7 %, Wald 87.6
%); at 80 % or 90 % it still catches 95.7 %. The cost: longer lines
(wider intervals).
0 yeses: from 0 to 1 - (α/2)^(1/n), 0.168 at n = 20 and 95 %.
Tap such a line: the panel shows that end as the CAS writes it.

RiskLab: RiskLab help 1/8: Logistic regression
A risk tool turns facts about a person into a
score that predicts an outcome Y (1 = re-
arrested, 0 = not).  Logistic regression:
ln(P/(1 - P)) = b₀ + b₁x₁ + ... + bk xk
odds = P/(1 - P); OR = e^b multiplies the odds
for +1 in x, the other x held fixed.
Fit: Newton-Raphson (IRLS), b → b + I^-1 U,
U = X'(y - μ), I = X'WX, W = μ(1 - μ),
until each step < 1E-9 (Hosmer & Lemeshow
2000; Agresti 2013).  SE = √(diag. of I^-1).
Wald z = b/SE.  LR χ² = 2(lnL - lnL₀), df k.
McFadden R² = 1 - lnL/lnL₀ (McFadden 1974):
not a share of variance explained.

RiskLab help 4/8: Cut-offs and trade-offs
A lower cut-off flags more people: more TP (sensitivity up) and
more FP (specificity down).  No cut-off avoids both errors.
PPV = TP/(TP + FP): of those flagged, the share with Y = 1.  It
depends on the base rate: the same sensitivity and specificity
give a lower PPV where Y = 1 is rarer.
NPV = TN/(TN + FN).
Choosing a cut-off is choosing which error matters more: the
statistics show the trade-off, but they cannot say which error
is worse.

r, the correlation, says how closely the

ScatterLab help 2/6: r², the share explained
All variation in y: SST = sum (y - ȳ)², the squared distances of
the points from the flat line at ȳ.

SurvLab: SurvLab help 1/5: Kaplan-Meier curves
Each man is followed until re-arrest (the event,
1) or until follow-up ends (censored, 0).  Rossi's
men were followed 52 weeks; 318 were not re-
arrested: we only know their time is over 52.
At each event time t, with d events among the n
at risk (not yet re-arrested, still followed):
S(t) = S(before t) × (1 - d/n)
the product-limit estimate (Kaplan & Meier 1958).
A censored man counts in n up to his last week,
then leaves: he is never counted as an event.
Greenwood (1926): Var S = S² × sum of d/(n(n - d)).
Ticks on the curve mark censoring times.

SurvLab help 2/5: CIs, median, quantiles
95% CI, log-log (default): S^exp(±1.96 √V/|ln S|), V = sum of
d/(n(n - d)); it stays inside 0..1.
Linear (soft key CI): S ± 1.96 SE, cut at 0 and 1.
Median: the first time S(t) < 0.5 (statsmodels;
SAS and R average if S sits exactly on 0.5).
If S never gets below 0.5 it is NOT REACHED: in Rossi only 26%
are re-arrested in 52 weeks.  Then report the time by which
25%, 20% or 10% are re-arrested (25%: S = 0.75, the 25th
percentile, or first quartile, of the time to re-arrest).
CI of a quantile (Brookmeyer & Crowley 1982): the event times
whose band reaches S = 1 - p, up to the next event time (not
included); n.r. (not reached) = no upper end.
Cumulative hazard H(t) = sum of d/n (Nelson-Aalen).

SurvLab help 3/5: Comparing two groups
Log-rank: at each event time, if both groups
shared one curve, group 1 would expect
E₁ = d × n₁/n of the d events.  O = observed.
χ² = (O₁ - E₁)²/V, df 1 (Mantel 1966).
HR = (O₁/E₁)/(O₂/E₂): below 1 = a lower hazard
in group 1; CI exp(ln HR ± 1.96√(1/E₁ + 1/E₂)).
Peto's HR exp((O₁ - E₁)/V) agrees with the test.
Gehan-Breslow weighs each time by n at risk:
early differences count more.  Log-rank is best
for proportional hazards.  Page 3's early/late
line is SurvLab's rule of thumb, not a test.
Assumes: censoring unrelated to the risk; for
the HR, curves that do not cross.

SurvLab help 4/5: The actuarial life table
Intervals [t, t + w) of the width you choose.
n = still at risk at the interval's start,
wdrn = withdrawn (censored) inside it,
n' = n - wdrn/2: a withdrawal is taken to be

TDist3D: TDist3D help 1/4: What the surface is
When σ is unknown, s takes its place in t = ( − μ) / (s/√n), and
s is a different number in every sample: t varies more than z
does, and the extra variation goes into the tails.
Student's t has one parameter, the degrees of freedom ν = n − 1.

ν runs away from you, 0.5 at the front to 10 at the back; the
height is the density f(t; ν).
Every curve has area 1.  The front curves (small ν) are low in the
middle and high in the tails; the back curves come close to
N(0,1), the normal curve, drawn as gray dots beyond the back
edge (ν = ∞).

Exposure levels have an ORDER (dose, hours, grade).  Pearson's

really do lie near a straight line.

proportions are from a straight line; a large value means they do
not follow one.

scores are spaced; Pearson's does not.  The Scores key switches
